Fixed **#393** (opencensus AzureLogHandler `lock=None` on Py3.13) en route. **GHCR package→repo connect done** (Actions-access grant → CI's `GITHUB_TOKEN` can push) and the **Deploy workflow validated end-to-end** (#403 fixed the migrate-command + frontend-pnpm bugs #401/#402; build→push→`alembic upgrade head`→ACA roll + SWA deploy all green on `v6`). **Post-deploy hardening (2026-06-28):** two production bugs surfaced and fixed — **#405** (Celery beat crashed on startup: the embedded `worker -B` beat re-nulled `self.lock` inside the opencensus `AzureLogHandler.createLock` fork on Python 3.13, silently killing ALL periodic tasks — orchestration polling, scheduled-suite dispatch, gap recovery, and sample-failure purge; fixed by making `createLock` idempotent in `backend/app/core/logging.py` + a network-free regression test; **#407** merged) and **#406** (deployed app couldn't read Key Vault: `AzureKeyVaultStore` called `DefaultAzureCredential()` with no args but the api+worker container runs a USER-assigned managed identity and `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` was unset — blocked connection tests, suite runs, AND orchestration polling; fixed by adding `AZURE_CLIENT_ID = azurerm_user_assigned_identity.app.client_id` to `local.app_env` in `deploy/terraform/azure/containerapps.tf`; **#408** merged). Backend image `:v7` built+pushed from main (with #405+#406); api+worker rolled to v7; App Insights re-enabled on the worker (the #405 mitigation of temporarily dropping `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` on the worker is reverted) — landed as **#409** (`image_tag` default v4→v7). **Orchestration polling is now live end-to-end** — beat starts clean (zero NoneType crashes) with App Insights on, api healthy (401, auth-enforced), ADF+Airflow connections polling via the 10-min beat fallback, Key Vault secrets read successfully. **Post-deploy feature batch (2026-06-29, all merged; prod image `:v7`→`:v10`):** Slack + email alert publishers behind the `ResultPublisher` seam (#413, `:v8`), column-aware failing-sample redaction (#417) + the #383/#384/#395/#423 hardening batch (`:v9`, bump #414), URL-encode DB password (#421/#395), always-alert operationally-failed runs (#419), alerting upsert race fix (#420/#384), per-run check outcome in the runs table (#425/#423), mypy gate over `backend/tests` (#418), and — **pulling ADR 0012 post-v1 Theme A forward — freshness & volume monitor-kinds end-to-end** (run engine #426 + authoring path & check-editor UI #437, `:v10`, bump #438). Three post-v1 design docs landed (#422/#430/#436) and are consolidated in **[context/post-v1-roadmap.md](context/post-v1-roadmap.md)** (the single post-v1 home + week-wise-task-generator input). **W7 in-repo work now DONE:** the **FastMCP 8-tool server** at `/mcp` (Azure-AD `JWTVerifier`-validated, fail-closed; ADR 0008, #460); the **hardening/docs pass** — prod-docs gate (#464), Swagger completeness + error-shape audit (#465), deployment guide + complete env-var reference (#468); **consistency hardening** — trigger-dedup index (#456, closes #308) + stuck-run reaper (#458, closes #309); the **visual-fidelity pass** (#459); and the W1–6 deferred + not-started triages (#463/#467, closing #169/#170). **Remaining W7 (external/coordination):** the Azure Monitor→ADF webhook alert rule, team onboarding, and discharging the deferred live warehouse/file + Claude-Desktop E2E smoke against the now-live harness (DataQ-side verified runs in progress). Week-6 close: the **alerting backend track** — `ResultPublisher` seam (#366), Teams adaptive card + publisher (#367), severity-aware routing (#368), dedup (#369), suppression/snooze (#370), per-suite notification config (#373) — plus the **prototype Phase 5–6 screens**: Profile content (#374), Workspace Settings (#375), Admin layout-reconcile (#376), standard 4xx/5xx error pages (#377), and the per-suite **notification config UI** (#378). Earlier Week-6: Results scaffold (PR-C1), Enhanced Monitoring Dashboard + run-detail route (#333), results filter bar + orchestration poll/correlation (#347), drawer→page restructures (#350), layout/prototype-fidelity polish (#353), and redacted sample failing rows (#365, closed #226). **Week-7 early-credit:** Azure deploy scaffolding (#379 — frontend Dockerfile + ACA/SWA manifests + parameterized deploy workflow + CORS middleware + prod env reference; manual-trigger only, the actual apply stays blocked on Azure RP registration per ADR 0021). _All Week-6 feature work **merged to `main`** as the stacked PR chain #366→#379; follow-ups #380 (W6 close-out docs), #381 (deploy migration-gate + doc reconcile — a Week-7 CI/CD task landed early), and #390 (live run-progress per-status histogram fix, closes #316) merged after._ **Cloud-neutral cutover (2026-07-01, ADR 0028 §5 — DONE):** the deployed frontend moved **Static Web App → a Container App** (`dataq-app-frontend`), now the **sole public surface**, running the one generic nginx image with runtime `DATAQ_AUTH_*` OIDC config (**MSAL retired** for a generic oidc-client-ts; validated live as Olivia → dashboard). The **api moved to internal ingress** (reached only via the frontend nginx proxy `/api` + `/mcp` + `/healthz`); the SWA (`dataq-app-web`) is **destroyed**. Landed as **#509** (cutover) → **#510** (lifecycle guards — `ignore_changes` on container images so applies never roll prod back to `var.image_tag`, + on the api `identifier_uris` so applies never strip the token audience) → **#511** (three ACA gotchas: nginx must proxy **HTTP/1.1** or ACA ingress 426s; api ingress **HTTP + `allow_insecure_connections`**; **orphaned SWA-EasyAuth** on the api disabled via `az containerapp auth update --enabled false` — it 401'd every request post-SWA-destroy; DataQ does its own `fastapi-azure-auth` validation). Prod frontend image `:v2`; URL `https://dataq-app-frontend.purplefield-f7322a1b.westus2.azurecontainerapps.io`. Follow-up **#512** (multi-arch frontend QEMU build impractically slow → `:latest` multi-arch unpublished; prod uses amd64). AWS/GCP deploy IaC stays post-v1 (#505).

# DataQ harness — live test/demo-data environment

External, **not-git-tracked** companion to DataQ (ADR 0021). Stands up a real retail
data environment in Azure + Snowflake + Databricks that exercises every DataQ run path
and both orchestration providers end-to-end, so the standing *"deferred live
warehouse/file run smoke"* can be discharged.

> Secrets live only in `secrets.sh` (chmod 600, never committed) and Terraform state
> (gitignored). Tracker: `../DataQ/HARNESS_TODO.md`.

---

## What's deployed

```
                         Azure (RG: dataq-rg)
  ADLS Gen2 (landing/raw) ── source-of-truth landing zone
        ▲  writes                         reads ▼
  Container Apps Environment (westus2)            Snowflake (AWS) — DATAQ_DB.RETAIL
   • mockdata cron Jobs (orders/tracking/             (12 tables; DATAQ_LOADER writes,
     inventory/feedback/supply) → ADLS                 DATAQ_READER reads)
   • Airflow: scheduler+webserver, CeleryExecutor   Databricks (AWS) — UC dataq_retail
   • Airflow Celery workers (scalable, 2 replicas)     reference / raw / silver / gold
   • Redis (Celery broker, internal TCP)              (serverless SQL warehouse)
   • ACR (images)                                   ADF (dataq-harness-adf)
  Postgres Flexible Server (westus3) — Airflow metadata   • event + timer pipelines
```

## Orchestration matrix (both providers × both trigger modalities)

| | Event-driven | Timer / schedule |
|---|---|---|
| **ADF** | `pl_flow_a_orders` (blob-event trigger) → Snowflake `ORDERS_HEADER` | `pl_flow_a_customers` (schedule trigger) → Snowflake `CUSTOMERS` |
| **Airflow** | `flow_a_payments_event` (Event Grid **push**: ADLS BlobCreated → receiver → REST `dagRuns`) → Snowflake `PAYMENTS` | `flow_a_snowflake_load` (9 feeds) + `flow_a_uc_reference` (8 dims) + `flow_b_medallion` (bronze→silver→gold) |

**Decoupled from DataQ by design:** orchestrators run *pure ETL* — no push to DataQ.
DataQ (one of several possible monitors) discovers runs by **polling** the ADF/Airflow
REST APIs (ADR 0006/0007). No `NotifyDataQ` web activity; no Airflow callback.

## Data model — 24 datasets / route map
See `mockdata/README.md`. Retail core (products, customers, orders header+lines,
payments, refunds, returns) + extended domain (settlements, purchase_orders+suppliers,
order_fulfillment+fulfillment_nodes, categories, date_dim, exchange_rates, discounts,
cancellations) + medallion sources (sales_events, feedback) + flat-files (tracking,
inventory). 18 deliberate DQ issues seeded for DataQ to catch (`_dq_issues_manifest.json`).

## Security / least-privilege
- **Snowflake:** `DATAQ_LOADER` (CREATE TABLE + write DML — ETL) vs `DATAQ_READER`
  (USAGE + SELECT — DataQ). Same user, role-switched. PII (`customers.email/phone`).
- **Databricks/UC:** loads run as the admin PAT (catalog owner); silver hashes the
  feedback email (#226). *Read/write split TODO:* a true least-priv read needs a
  **separate service principal** with SELECT-only grants (UC grants are per-principal,
  and the harness has one PAT) — recommended but not yet implemented; Snowflake is the
  reference pattern.
- Auth posture: key-based throughout (account keys / SAS / PAT) — accepted for a
  disposable harness; the Contributor SP can't create the role assignments that
  managed-identity/RBAC would need.

> AGENT

I dug into the live harness (`dataq-rg`). Here's the real state on both questions.

## 1. Are the file-generation cron jobs running regularly?

**They fire on schedule, but every run is failing — so no files are actually being generated.**

Five `mockdata-*` Container Apps Jobs are deployed and triggering on cron:

| Job | Schedule | Recent executions |
|---|---|---|
| mockdata-orders | `0 0,6,12,18 * * *` (every 6h) | **all Failed** |
| mockdata-tracking | `0 0,12 * * *` | **all Failed** |
| mockdata-inventory | `0 1 * * *` | **all Failed** |
| mockdata-supply | `30 0 * * *` | **all Failed** |
| mockdata-feedback | `0 1 */2 * *` | **all Failed** |

Every execution since 2026-06-29 dies with:
```
FileNotFoundError: no state found — run `python -m mockdata init` first
```

**Root cause:** the jobs run `tick` (incremental), which needs persistent state (`state/state.json` + master pools) that `mockdata init` creates **once** in ADLS. That `state/` path **does not exist** — `init` was never run against ADLS. So the incremental generator has never produced a single file; the schedule is just failing on a loop.

What *does* exist in ADLS is a one-time **`backfill`** someone landed manually (`snowflake/`, `unity_catalog/`, `adls_flatfile/`, `databricks_medallion/` + `_manifest.json` + `_dq_issues_manifest.json`) — a static initial dataset, nothing fresh since.

## 2. Did we test the seeded deliberate DQ issues?

**Generation: yes. DataQ catching them end-to-end: not confirmed.**

- The **18 issues are generated and landed** — `_dq_issues_manifest.json` in ADLS confirms all 18, and they were verified locally against the manifest (HARNESS_TODO line 112 `[x]`). They cover exactly what you listed: `null` (orders_header.channel, customers.email) · `duplicate` (order_lines rows, products PK) · `fk_orphan` (**SKU-000000**, **CUST-000000**, CAT-0000, SUP-0000, NODE-0000) · `reconciliation` (order_total vs lines, payments underpayment, settlements, PO qty) · `stale` + `volume_drop` + `schema_drift` (inventory_snapshot) · `consistency` (cancellations) · `completeness` (date_dim).
- **But there's no evidence DataQ actually ran against this and flagged them** — that's the still-deferred "live warehouse/file smoke" + the QA/QE §4 assertion, and the tracker doesn't tick it. Worse, the **tick-dependent** issues (freshness / volume-drop / schema-drift, which need successive daily snapshots) can't be exercised at all while the tick jobs fail — only the static backfill snapshot is catchable point-in-time.

## The fix
It's a harness operational gap, not a DataQ bug: run **`mockdata init`** once against ADLS to seed the state, after which the tick crons will succeed and start landing incremental data. Simplest path — locally with the connection string from `secrets.sh`:
```
AZURE_STORAGE_CONNECTION_STRING=... python -m mockdata init \
  --out adls://dataqharness3erlgd/landing \
  --state adls://dataqharness3erlgd/landing/state
```

Want me to run the `init` against the live harness to unblock the crons? (It writes state + reference loads to ADLS — a one-time bootstrap on the shared harness, so I'd rather confirm before touching it.) I can also update `HARNESS_TODO.md` to record this finding either way.

## What was wrong & what I did

**The cron jobs were firing on schedule but 100% failing** since 2026-06-29 — every `tick` died with `FileNotFoundError: no state found`. Root cause: `init` seeds shared state (masters + counters) into ADLS `…/landing/state`, and that state had been lost when the storage/landing was recreated after the original 2026-06-27 seed — and never re-run. So the schedule was looping on failure, landing **zero** incremental data (only the old static backfill remained).

**Fix (validated):**
1. Re-ran `init` through the **exact job image** (`docker run --platform linux/amd64 … mockdata:latest init …`) → state re-seeded (masters + reference dims + `state.json`).
2. Kicked all five feeds via `az containerapp job start` → **`orders`/`tracking`/`inventory`/`feedback`/`supply` all now `Succeeded`**, landing fresh `*_b*.csv` batches and appending `_ticks.jsonl`.

The scheduled runs will now succeed on their normal cadence (orders every 6h, tracking 2×/day, inventory + supply daily, feedback every 2 days).

## Your two questions, answered

1. **Running regularly?** They *fire* regularly, but had been failing every time — now unblocked and confirmed working across all 5 feeds.
2. **Seeded DQ issues tested?** The **generation** is verified — all **18** issues (nulls · dupes · FK orphans SKU-000000/CUST-000000/CAT-0000/SUP-0000/NODE-0000 · reconciliation mismatches · stale freshness · volume drop · schema drift · consistency · completeness) are in `_dq_issues_manifest.json` and were validated against the manifest locally. But **DataQ actually catching them end-to-end is still not confirmed** — that's the deferred live-smoke + the §4 QA/QE assertion, and notably the freshness/volume/schema-drift ones need the now-restored tick cadence to accumulate successive snapshots.

Updated `HARNESS_TODO.md` (§2a) with the incident, the fix, and a **recurrence guard** follow-up: the tick jobs fail-hard on missing state with no auto-recovery, so a future storage-wipe silently breaks the crons again. I flagged options — make `tick` auto-`init`, add a one-shot `mockdata-init` job post-apply, and/or alert on repeated job-execution failures.

=== issue #415 body ===
Actionable failing-row samples: column-aware redaction (classify PII vs identifier vs safe), not blanket masking
OPEN
## Problem
`redact_sample_failures` (`backend/app/services/run_service.py`) **blanket-masks every value** in `partial_unexpected_list`, keeping only `unexpected_count`/`unexpected_percent`. So a failing-row sample shows column *names* but `<redacted>` for **every** value — including the **offending value** (e.g. `LINE_TOTAL`, not PII) and the **identifier** (e.g. `ORDER_NUMBER`). The sample is unactionable: you can't see *what* was wrong or *which* row, which defeats the purpose.

The blanket approach was a deliberate safe default ("can't enumerate which columns are PII ahead of time") — secure but blunt. Only PII should be redacted, and a real identifier must survive.

## Fix — column-aware, surgical redaction
Classify each target column, then show the safe ones and redact only PII (default-redact anything unclassified, so security never regresses):

**Detection precedence**
1. **Datasource classification/tags** (authoritative): Snowflake `privacy_category` (`IDENTIFIER`/`QUASI_IDENTIFIER`/`SENSITIVE`) via classification/tags; Unity Catalog column tags (`system.information_schema.column_tags`).
2. **Column-name heuristics** (fallback): reuse `core.logging._PII_KEYS` (email/ssn/phone/name/...).
3. **Manual override** stored as **suite-level metadata** — `identifier_column` + `pii_columns` (nullable; shaped to promote to a connection/column catalog later).
4. **Default-redact** unclassified.

**Redaction policy (new)**
- Always show the **identifier column** (must be non-PII) so the row is locatable.
- Show the **check's tested column** (the metric that failed) unless tagged PII.
- Redact PII columns + unclassified columns.
- The retention-sweep PII purge (`purge_expired_sample_failures`) is unchanged.

## Surfacing
Run-detail drill-down + the Slack/email sample show the now-actionable rows (`ORDER-1041 · line_total = −12.50`). Sibling issue: richer notifications.

## Sequencing
1. Suite-level metadata (`identifier_column`, `pii_columns`) — backward-compatible migration.
2. Column-aware redaction using name-heuristics + manual override (keeps default-redact fallback).
3. Datasource-native classification (Snowflake/UC) as the authoritative layer.
4. Run-detail + notification surfacing.

Found while validating a real failing run (the seeded LINE_TOTAL breach showed `<redacted>` for the value + identifier).

Both are great questions. Here's the accurate state from the code.

## 1. Freshness alert — implemented, but wouldn't have fired for *this*

Freshness monitoring **is** implemented (ADR 0012 Theme A, #426/#437) — [monitors.py](backend/app/datasources/monitors.py): config `{"column": <timestamp col>}`, metric = **age in hours**, it *requires* a fail/critical age threshold (rejected otherwise, so it can't ship silently green — [check_service.py:148](backend/app/services/check_service.py#L148)), and a breach flows through the same severity → `ResultPublisher` alert path as any check ([run_service.py:98](backend/app/services/run_service.py#L98)).

But no alert fired for the cron outage, for two reasons:

- **DataQ monitors *data* freshness, not the harness's job health.** It has no view of the `mockdata-*` Container App Jobs. It would only notice the stopped source *indirectly* — a freshness check on, say, `inventory_snapshot` seeing `max(load_ts)` age climb past the threshold. There's no infra-health watch on the jobs themselves.
- **Nothing is wired against the live harness data yet.** That's exactly the still-deferred "live warehouse/file smoke" + the §4 QA/QE assertion we flagged earlier — no suite/schedule currently runs a freshness check on the harness datasets, so there was nothing to detect it.

The irony is useful: the outage I just fixed *created real staleness* (no new snapshots for ~3 days), so a wired freshness check **would** have caught it — both that and the deliberately-seeded `+26h` `inventory_snapshot` issue. It just needs to be authored + scheduled. **So: implemented, not yet wired/tested E2E.**

## 2. Sample identifier column — partially; the engine landed, the plumbing didn't

This is issue **#415**, still **OPEN**. #417 shipped *part* of it:

**Done (#417):** the redaction *engine* is column-aware — [`redact_sample_failures`](backend/app/services/run_service.py#L525) keeps the **identifier column** + the **tested column** and default-masks everything else (PII or unclassified), and the `Suite` model has the policy field `{"identifier_column", "pii_columns"}` ([models.py:206](backend/app/db/models.py#L206)).

**Not done (why #415 stays open):**
- **No way to set it.** Grep for `identifier_column`/`pii_columns` in `backend/app/api`, `schemas`, and `frontend/src` → **nothing**. The policy column exists on the model but there's no API/UI to populate it, so in practice it's always `NULL` → the blanket-mask fallback.
- **The runner doesn't capture the identifier for standard checks.** [gx_runner.py](backend/app/datasources/gx_runner.py) only pulls `_SAMPLE_KEYS = ("partial_unexpected_list", "unexpected_count", "unexpected_percent")` — the failing *column's* scalar values, with **no** `unexpected_index_column_names` requested from GX. So for a null/dup/range check there's no row context to show an identifier from. The redactor even has an `unexpected_index_list` branch ready ([run_service.py:564](backend/app/services/run_service.py#L564)), but nothing populates it (only a custom-SQL `UnexpectedRowsExpectation` returns full rows).
- **Datasource-native classification** (Snowflake `privacy_category` / UC column tags — step 3) isn't implemented; only the name heuristic exists.

So: the *design* and the redaction half are in, but you **cannot currently get an identifier into a sample** — no setter, and the GX runner doesn't capture row keys for the common column-expectation path.

def classify_pii(row):
    column_name = row['COLUMN_NAME']
    sampled_values = row['SAMPLED_VALUES_P']
    
    pii_patterns = [
    '%name%', '%email%', '%phone%', '%mobile%', '%contact%', '%address%',
    '%street%', '%city%', '%state%', '%zip%', '%postal%', '%ssn%',
    '%social_security%', '%credit_card%', '%ccn%', '%bank%', '%passport%',
    '%license%', '%nid%', '%birth%', '%dob%', '%username%', '%user_id%',
    '%login%', '%fax%']
    
    non_pii_patterns = [
    '%_ts%', '%ts_%', '%time_%', '%_time%', '%_dt%', '%account%']

    def is_potential_hash(input):
        hash_lengths = {32,40,64,128}
        hex_pattern = re.compile(r'^[a-fA-F0-9]+$')
        if len(input) in hash_lengths and hex_pattern.match(input):
            return True
        else:
            return False

    def calculate_entropy(input):
        if not input:
            return 0
        length = len(input)
        char_count = {}
        for char in input:
            char_count[char] = char_count.get(char,0) + 1
        entropy = sum((-count / length) * log2(count/length) for count in char_count.values())
        return entropy

    def is_base64(input):
        base64_pattern = re.compile(r'^[A-Za-z0-9+/]+={0,2}$')
        return bool(base64_pattern.match(input))


    def is_hexadecimal(input):
        hex_pattern = re.compile(r'^[a-fA-F0-9]+$')
        return len(input) % 2 == 0 and bool(hex_pattern.match(input))

    def is_encrypted(input):
        entropy = calculate_entropy(input)
        non_alnum_chars = bool(re.search(r'[^\w\s]', input))

        return (
            (entropy > 3.5 and non_alnum_chars and (is_base64(input) or is_hexadecimal(input)))
            or is_potential_hash(input)
        )
        

    is_pii_like = any(pattern.strip('%').lower() in column_name.lower() for pattern in pii_patterns)
    is_non_pii_like = any(pattern.strip('%').lower() in column_name.lower() for pattern in non_pii_patterns)

    sampled_values_list = json.loads(sampled_values)
    
    encrypted_count = sum(is_encrypted(str(input)) for input in sampled_values_list if input and input != 'NULL')
    non_null_count = len([input for input in sampled_values if input])
    valid_records_ratio = encrypted_count / non_null_count if non_null_count else 0

    if valid_records_ratio >= 0.1:
        return "Encrypted"
    elif valid_records_ratio > 0 and valid_records_ratio < 0.1:
        if is_pii_like and not is_non_pii_like:
            return "Possibly Encrypted" 
        else:
            return "Not Encrypted"
    elif not non_null_count:
        if is_pii_like and not is_non_pii_like:
            return "Possibly Encrypted" 
        else:
            return "Not Encrypted"
    else:
        return "Not Encrypted" ###########NEED REVIEW
```

=== dataq_setup/README (how DataQ is wired to the harness) ===
# DataQ-side setup for the harness flows (§3)

The harness produces data + loads it; **DataQ** still needs its connections, suites,
checks, and trigger-bindings created so the flows actually run + alert. This is
*runtime* config against a **deployed DataQ** (it can't be done until DataQ is up and
the tables exist), so it lives here as a spec + a scaffold (`setup.py`), not Terraform.

Run after: Terraform applied · images pushed · a few mockdata Jobs + the Flow A/B
loads have populated the tables. Auth: `DATAQ_BASE_URL` + `DATAQ_TOKEN` (bearer).

> Connection/suite/check payloads are **spec-driven and version-specific** — verify
> each against DataQ's live OpenAPI (`$DATAQ_BASE_URL/docs`) before trusting it. The
> **trigger-bindings** below are exact (their `pipeline_or_dag_id` must match the DAG
> ids / ADF pipeline name this harness ships).

## Objects per flow

### Flow A — Snowflake (`flow_a_snowflake_load` DAG + `pl_flow_a_orders` ADF pipeline)
- **Connection** `snowflake` → `DATAQ_DB` / `RETAIL`, reads as `DATAQ_READER` (read-only, distinct from the loader role).
- **Suite** `flow_a_snowflake` over the loaded tables, with at least:
  - column expectations (not-null `order_number`, `qty > 0`, `unit_price >= 0`)
  - a **custom-SQL check** (ADR 0019) for the reconciliation:
    `SELECT order_number FROM orders_header h WHERE order_total <> (SELECT ROUND(SUM(line_total)*1.08,2) FROM order_lines l WHERE l.order_number=h.order_number)` → expect 0 rows
- **Trigger-bindings**: `(airflow, flow_a_snowflake_load, <env>)` **and** `(adf, pl_flow_a_orders, <env>)` → this suite.

### Flow A — Unity Catalog reference (`flow_a_uc_reference` DAG)
- **Connection** `unity_catalog` → catalog `dataq_retail`, schema `reference`.
- **Suite** `flow_a_uc_reference` (not-null keys, allowed `channel` set, FK-ish checks).
- **Trigger-binding**: `(airflow, flow_a_uc_reference, <env>)` → this suite.

### Flow B — medallion (`flow_b_medallion` DAG)
- **Connection** `unity_catalog` → catalog `dataq_retail`, schemas `silver` / `gold`.
- **Suites**: `flow_b_silver` (PII-redaction: `email` is hashed, dedup) and `flow_b_gold`
  (freshness on `daily_revenue`, volume band, non-negative revenue).
- **Trigger-binding**: `(airflow, flow_b_medallion, <env>)` → the gold suite.

### Flow C — flat-file in place (no orchestrator; DataQ runs on its own schedule)
- **Connection** `adls` (flat-file) → tracking, path `adls_flatfile/logistics_tracking/`,
  **batch pattern** `tracking_events_(.+)\.csv`, strategy `latest` (first capture group = batch key).
- **Connection** `adls` (flat-file) → inventory, path `adls_flatfile/inventory_snapshot/`,
  **batch pattern** `inventory_snapshot_(.+)\.parquet`, strategy `latest`.
- **Suites**: tracking (status in the lifecycle set, non-null `tracking_number`),
  inventory (`on_hand >= 0`, freshness on `load_ts`). Run via a DataQ **schedule**
  (Week-5 `schedules`) — no trigger-binding (nothing loads these).

## Trigger-binding summary (exact)

| provider | pipeline_or_dag_id | → suite |
|---|---|---|
| `airflow` | `flow_a_snowflake_load` | flow_a_snowflake |
| `airflow` | `flow_a_uc_reference` | flow_a_uc_reference |
| `airflow` | `flow_b_medallion` | flow_b_gold |
| `adf` | `pl_flow_a_orders` | flow_a_snowflake |

`env` is your DataQ environment label (e.g. `dev`). See `setup.py`.

Key finding: **freshness/volume monitors are SQL-only** — only Snowflake and UC implement `run_monitors`; `FlatFileCheckRunner` does **not**. > AGENT

Crucial detail confirmed: DataQ treats a naive Snowflake timestamp as **UTC** and clamps future timestamps to age 0 ([monitors.py:112-133](backend/app/datasources/monitors.py#L112)). So the Snowflake `-5h` `DATEDIFF` was just its session-TZ; DataQ will compute `ORDER_TS` age as ~now(UTC) − 17:57 ≈ **~1.8h**. That's a usable, real freshness signal — I'll author it and dry-run to read the exact age, then band the threshold to fail.

This ADLS suite can't host freshness, so let me delete it and create the freshness suite on **Snowflake — Orders**. Cancelling the check editor first:

And the alert delivery, confirmed from the worker logs:

- `email_alert_sent` also fired (workspace email publisher).

So the full chain works: **author freshness monitor → run → detect staleness (1.8h ≥ 1h fail threshold) → severity `fail` → Slack + email alert delivered.** The `metric_value` (1.801) is persisted as a numeric scalar too (ADR 0012 — trendable).

### Two things worth flagging

1. **Freshness/volume monitors are SQL-only.** Only the Snowflake and UC runners implement `run_monitors`; `FlatFileCheckRunner` doesn't. So DataQ **cannot** run a freshness monitor on the ADLS flat-file inventory — the harness's seeded *flat-file* freshness issue (`inventory_snapshot.load_ts +26h`) is currently **uncatchable** by the freshness monitor. That's a real gap (freshness on flat-files would need file-mtime or a read-max-`load_ts` path). Worth a GitHub issue — want me to file it?

2. **Demo suite left in place.** "Orders Freshness — Snowflake (harness demo)" is manual-run only (no schedule/trigger), so it won't re-alert or spam. It's a working freshness example — say the word if you'd rather I delete it.

A person entity + an id token (customer_id, user_key) → PII (re-identifies).\n    if has_id_token and (tokens & _PERSON_ENTITIES):\n        return ColumnClass.PII\n    # 3. Non-person identifier → SHOW as a locator.\n    if has_id_token:\n        return ColumnClass.IDENTIFIER\n    # 4. Metric / time / status → safe.\n    if tokens & _SAFE_TOKENS:\n        return ColumnClass.SAFE\n    return None\n\n\n# ── Value-shape signals (refine a name-inconclusive column) ─────────────────────\n\n_UUID_RE = re.compile(r\"^[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}$\")\n_HEX_RE = re.compile(r\"^[0-9a-fA-F]+$\")\n_BASE64_RE = re.compile(r\"^[A-Za-z0-9+/]+={0,2}$\")\n_HASH_LENGTHS = frozenset({32, 40, 56, 64, 96, 128})  # md5/sha1/sha224/sha256/sha384/sha512 hex\n\n\ndef _shannon_entropy(text: str) -> float:\n    \"\"\"Shannon entropy (bits/char) of a string — high for random/encoded blobs.\"\"\"\n    if not text:\n        return 0.0\n    counts: dict[str, int] = {}\n    for ch in text:\n        counts[ch] = counts.get(ch, 0) + 1\n    n = len(text)\n    return -sum((c / n) * math.log2(c / n) for c in counts.values())\n\n\ndef _looks_like_uuid(value: str) -> bool:\n    return bool(_UUID_RE.match(value))\n\n\ndef _looks_like_hash(value: str) -> bool:\n    \"\"\"A hex string of a common digest length (md5/sha*) — a hashed/opaque token.\"\"\"\n    return len(value) in _HASH_LENGTHS and bool(_HEX_RE.match(value))\n\n\ndef _looks_encoded(value: str) -> bool:\n    \"\"\"High-entropy base64/hex — an encrypted/encoded blob (treat as sensitive).\"\"\"\n    return (\n        len(value) >= 16\n        and _shannon_entropy(value) > 3.5\n        and bool(_BASE64_RE.match(value) or _HEX_RE.match(value))\n    )\n\n\ndef _clean_values(values: Iterable[object]) -> list[str]:\n    \"\"\"Non-null, non-empty sampled values as strings.\"\"\"\n    out: list[str] = []\n    for v in values:\n        if v is None:\n            continue\n        s = str(v).strip()\n        if s and s.upper() != \"NULL\":\n            out.append(s)\n    return out\n\n\ndef _value_signal(values: Sequence[object]) -> ColumnClass | None:\n    \"\"\"Classify from a column's sampled *values*, or ``None`` if inconclusive.\n\n    UUID/hash-shaped, near-unique values look like a machine identifier; a column of\n    high-entropy encoded blobs is treated as sensitive (PII-adjacent). A ratio (not\n    all-or-nothing) tolerates a few odd values in the sample.\"\"\"\n    cleaned = _clean_values(values)\n    if not cleaned:\n        return None\n    n = len(cleaned)\n    id_shaped = sum(_looks_like_uuid(v) or _looks_like_hash(v) for v in cleaned)\n    encoded = sum(_looks_encoded(v) for v in cleaned)\n    distinct_ratio = len(set(cleaned)) / n\n\n    if id_shaped / n >= 0.8 and distinct_ratio >= 0.8:\n        return ColumnClass.IDENTIFIER\n    if encoded / n >= 0.5:\n        return ColumnClass.PII\n    return None\n\n\ndef classify_column(name: str, sampled_values: Sequence[object] | None = None) -> ColumnClass:\n    \"\"\"Classify a column as IDENTIFIER / PII / SAFE for sample redaction (#415).\n\n    The column *name* is authoritative when it carries a known token; otherwise the\n    sampled *values* refine an unknown column. With neither conclusive, the result is\n    **PII** (conservative default-mask — security never regresses).\n\n    ``sampled_values`` are a small profile sample (a few rows); ``None``/empty falls\n    back to the name signal only.\n    \"\"\"\n    by_name = _name_signal(name)\n    if by_name is not None:\n        return by_name\n    by_value = _value_signal(sampled_values or [])\n    if by_value is not None:\n        return by_value\n    return ColumnClass.PII\n"
}

`backend/app/services/column_classification.py` + 46 tests (all pass; ruff/mypy/black/bandit clean), on branch `feature/415-column-classifier`.

It follows your pattern — name-token buckets + value-signal — but emits **`identifier` / `pii` / `safe`** instead of encryption states. Key calls (worth your eye, since you handed me the pattern):

| Rule | Example | Class |
|---|---|---|
| Person/sensitive name token | `email`, `home_address`, `date_of_birth` | **pii** |
| Person-linking id (re-identifies) | `customer_id`, `user_id` | **pii** |
| Non-person id-suffix | `order_number`, `sku`, `tracking_number` | **identifier** |
| `name` on a non-person entity | `product_name`, `category_name` | **safe** |
| `name` otherwise | `customer_name` | **pii** |
| Metric/time/status | `load_ts`, `line_total`, `status` | **safe** |
| Value shape (name unknown) | UUID/sha-hex, high-cardinality | **identifier** |
| Value shape | high-entropy base64/hex blobs | **pii** |
| **Default (unknown)** | `wibble` | **pii** (conservative — never regresses masking) |

Two adaptations from your original I want to flag: I kept **entity nouns out of the id-token set** (so `order_ts` reads as a timestamp, not an id), and I treat the **conservative default as PII/mask** (your `NEED REVIEW` branch returned "Not Encrypted" — I went the safe-by-default way for a redactor).

### Remaining (b) increments (planned, on this branch → one PR)
2. **Derive the policy** — auto-fill `Suite.sample_redaction_policy` (`identifier_column` + `pii_columns`) by running the classifier over a column profile; wire it into `redact_sample_failures`.
3. **Capture the identifier** — set GX `unexpected_index_column_names` in `gx_runner` so a sample actually contains the identifier value (the real functional gap — today `partial_unexpected_list` is only the failing column's scalars).
4. **Setter** — API + check/suite UI to set/override the policy.

I'll keep building 2 → 3 → 4 on this branch and open one PR when it delivers end-to-end. Before I go further: **any changes to the classification rules above** (token vocabularies, the person-id-as-PII call, or the PII default)? If they look right, I'll proceed with increment 2.

> DEVELOPER

customer_id, user_id these should be identifier, no? [as these are kind of surrogate key]
correct me if I'm wrong

> AGENT

You're right, and it's a good correction. Let me reason it out so we're aligned:

A surrogate key like `customer_id = 4471` (or a UUID) is exactly the **row locator** you want in a failing sample — that's its job — and it's the *pseudonymized* form: it doesn't leak a name/email/phone, it just points. Masking it defeats the whole purpose of an "actionable sample." So defaulting it to **identifier** is the right call.

The one nuance to preserve: a person-linking id is still personal data in the strict GDPR sense (Art 4(1) names "an identification number"), and occasionally a "*_id*" column is actually a **natural key that IS PII** — e.g., `user_id` whose values are emails/usernames. So:
- **Name says id → treat as IDENTIFIER** (surrogate key, show it), but
- **if the values look like emails, keep it PII** (a natural key leaking a direct identifier must not be shown), and
- the explicit `pii_columns` override / datasource tags remain the authoritative escape hatch for orgs that must mask even pseudonymous keys.

Let me make that change.

236	    r"^[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}$"

239	_BASE64_RE = re.compile(r"^[A-Za-z0-9+/]+={0,2}$")

242	
243	def _shannon_entropy(text: str) -> float:
244	    """Shannon entropy (bits/char) of a string — high for random/encoded blobs."""
245	    if not text:
246	        return 0.0
247	    counts: dict[str, int] = {}
248	    for ch in text:
249	        counts[ch] = counts.get(ch, 0) + 1
250	    n = len(text)
251	    return -sum((c / n) * math.log2(c / n) for c in counts.values())
252	
253	
254	def _looks_like_uuid(value: str) -> bool:
255	    return bool(_UUID_RE.match(value))
256	
257	
258	def _looks_like_hash(value: str) -> bool:
259	    """A hex string of a common digest length (md5/sha*) — a hashed/opaque token."""
260	    return len(value) in _HASH_LENGTHS and bool(_HEX_RE.match(value))
261	
262	
263	def _looks_encoded(value: str) -> bool:
264	    """High-entropy base64/hex — an encrypted/encoded blob (treat as sensitive)."""
265	    return (
266	        len(value) >= 16
267	        and _shannon_entropy(value) > 3.5
268	        and bool(_BASE64_RE.match(value) or _HEX_RE.match(value))
269	    )

272	def _clean_values(values: Iterable[object]) -> list[str]:
273	    """Non-null, non-empty sampled values as strings."""
274	    out: list[str] = []
275	    for v in values:
276	        if v is None:
277	            continue
278	        s = str(v).strip()
279	        if s and s.upper() != "NULL":
280	            out.append(s)
281	    return out

284	def _value_signal(values: Sequence[object]) -> ColumnClass | None:
285	    """Classify from a column's sampled *values*, or ``None`` if inconclusive.
286	
287	    UUID/hash-shaped, near-unique values look like a machine identifier; a column of
288	    high-entropy encoded blobs is treated as sensitive (PII-adjacent). A ratio (not
289	    all-or-nothing) tolerates a few odd values in the sample."""
290	    cleaned = _clean_values(values)
291	    if not cleaned:
292	        return None
293	    n = len(cleaned)
294	    id_shaped = sum(_looks_like_uuid(v) or _looks_like_hash(v) for v in cleaned)
295	    encoded = sum(_looks_encoded(v) for v in cleaned)
296	    distinct_ratio = len(set(cleaned)) / n
297	
298	    if id_shaped / n >= 0.8 and distinct_ratio >= 0.8:
299	        return ColumnClass.IDENTIFIER
300	    if encoded / n >= 0.5:
301	        return ColumnClass.PII
302	    return None
303

305	def classify_column(name: str, sampled_values: Sequence[object] | None = None) -> ColumnClass:
306	    """Classify a column as IDENTIFIER / PII / SAFE for sample redaction (#415).
307	
308	    The column *name* is authoritative when it carries a known token; otherwise the
309	    sampled *values* refine an unknown column. With neither conclusive, the result is
310	    **PII** (conservative default-mask — security never regresses).
311	
312	    ``sampled_values`` are a small profile sample (a few rows); ``None``/empty falls
313	    back to the name signal only.
314	    """

With neither conclusive, the result is\n    **PII** (conservative default-mask — security never regresses).\n\n    ``sampled_values`` are a small profile sample (a few rows); ``None``/empty falls\n    back to the name signal only.\n    \"\"\"\n    by_name = _name_signal(name)\n    if by_name is not None:\n        return by_name\n    by_value = _value_signal(sampled_values or [])\n    if by_value is not None:\n        return by_value\n    return ColumnClass.PII",
  "new_string": "    \"\"\"Classify a column as IDENTIFIER / PII / SAFE for sample redaction (#415).\n\n    Precedence:\n    1. A **PII name** → PII (always mask).\n    2. **Directly-sensitive values** (emails, encoded blobs) → PII — this *overrides* a\n       name that looks like an identifier, so a natural key holding PII (a ``user_id``\n       column of emails) is masked, not shown.\n    3. The **name** signal (IDENTIFIER / SAFE) when it carried a known token.\n    4. The **value** signal (IDENTIFIER) for a name-inconclusive column.\n    5. Otherwise **PII** — conservative default-mask, so security never regresses.\n\n    ``sampled_values`` are a small profile sample (a few rows); ``None``/empty falls\n    back to the name signal only.\n    \"\"\"\n    by_name = _name_signal(name)\n    if by_name is ColumnClass.PII:\n        return ColumnClass.PII\n    by_value = _value_signal(sampled_values or [])\n    if by_value is ColumnClass.PII:  # sensitive values override a name-based identifier\n        return ColumnClass.PII\n    if by_name is not None:  # IDENTIFIER or SAFE\n        return by_name\n    if by_value is not None:  # IDENTIFIER\n        return by_value\n    return ColumnClass.PII"

> AGENT

You were right — corrected. `customer_id` / `user_id` now classify as **identifier**.

The reasoning, so we're on the same page: a surrogate/pseudonymous key is exactly the row locator you want to show, and it doesn't leak a direct identifier — it just points. Masking it would defeat the "actionable sample" goal. It's still personal data in the strict GDPR sense, but showing the *pseudonym* is far lower-risk than showing a name/email, and that's the whole point of pseudonymization.

I kept one guard so we don't lose the edge case: a **value-level PII signal overrides the name** — so a `user_id` column whose *values* are actually emails (a natural key leaking a direct identifier) still classifies as **pii** and gets masked. And the explicit `pii_columns` override / datasource tags remain the authoritative overrule for orgs that must mask even pseudonymous keys.

Tests now cover both: `customer_id`/`user_id` with opaque values → identifier; `user_id` holding emails → pii. All 48 green (ruff/mypy/black/bandit clean), folded into the increment-1 commit.

Next up is **increment 2** — derive the suite policy (`identifier_column` + `pii_columns`) from the classifier over a column profile and wire it into `redact_sample_failures`. Want me to proceed, or any other classification calls to adjust first (e.g. the token vocabularies, or should business-entity names like `supplier_name` be safe vs masked)?

> DEVELOPER

one point, the approach we are doing for the identifier and PII currently should be set at level two. First level is the, databases tags. Then tis approach. And the last stage would be the user override. Is my understanding correct?

> AGENT

Yes — your three-layer model is exactly the #415 design, and the classifier we just built **is** level 2. The only thing I'd make explicit is the *direction* of authority, because "first vs last" can be read two ways.

## The resolution stack (per column)

| Layer | Source | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Datasource tags** | Snowflake `privacy_category`, UC column tags | Authoritative source-of-truth from data governance |
| **2. Heuristic** *(built)* | name + value classifier | Fallback when the column isn't tagged |
| **3. User override** | suite `pii_columns` / `identifier_column` | The human's final say |
| **4. Default** | — | Mask (nothing said → conservative) |

So the pipeline order is tags → heuristic → override → default, exactly as you said. The one clarification on **who wins when they disagree**:

- **Choosing the identifier:** the **override is highest authority** (a person's explicit "this is the locator" beats a guess), then tags, then heuristic. That's what "override is the last stage" means — it's applied last and gets the final word.
- **Masking PII: treat it as additive/monotonic — a *union*, not a last-wins.** A column is masked if **any** layer says sensitive (tag OR heuristic OR override). This matters for compliance: a suite owner's override should be able to *add* masking, and to *un-mask a heuristic false positive*, but it should **not** be able to un-mask a column that **datasource governance tagged sensitive**. Otherwise a suite owner could expose PII the DBA deliberately locked down.

So the precise rule I'd implement:
- `masked = tag_sensitive ∪ heuristic_pii ∪ override_pii`, **minus** `override_show` — but `override_show` can only lift a *heuristic* PII flag, never a *tag* one (governance wins on masking).
- `identifier = override_identifier` if set and not masked, else the tag/heuristic pick, and it must be non-PII.

Net: **your understanding is correct.** The only refinement is that "override last" = highest authority for the *identifier*, while for *PII masking* the layers **union** (safe-by-default) with a governance-tag floor the override can't cross.

Two things for you to confirm before I wire level 2 into the policy (increment 2), since they're policy calls:
1. **Should a user override be allowed to un-mask a *datasource-tagged* sensitive column?** My recommendation: **no** (governance floor); it can only un-mask heuristic false positives.
2. Level 1 (datasource tags) and level 3 (override setter) are their own increments after this — fine to keep building level 2's wiring now and add 1 & 3 after?

531	    """Redact a result's `sample_failures` for safe surfacing on the read API.
532	
533	    `sample_failures` carries aggregate counts plus `partial_unexpected_list` —
534	    the failing values of the **tested column** — and (when a future runner records
535	    it) an `unexpected_index_list` of failing rows. Suite-level ``view`` authz lets
536	    share-recipients read a suite's results, so PII must not cross that boundary
537	    unredacted (CLAUDE.md PII rule; purged on the retention sweep below).
538	
539	    Column-aware policy (#415) — surgical, not blanket:
540	    * numeric summary keys (`unexpected_count` / `unexpected_percent`) always pass;
541	    * `partial_unexpected_list` (the tested column's failing values) passes when
542	      ``tested_column`` is **not** PII — per the suite ``policy.pii_columns`` or the
543	      name heuristic — so a non-PII breach (e.g. a bad ``LINE_TOTAL``) is finally
544	      *visible*, while a PII tested column (``email``) stays masked;
545	    * `unexpected_index_list` row-dicts are masked **per column** (identifier +
546	      non-PII shown, PII masked);
547	    * everything else default-masks (unclassified → redacted, so security can't
548	      regress).
549	
550	    With neither ``tested_column`` nor ``policy`` the legacy **blanket mask** is
551	    kept (the safe default for callers that don't know the column) — only the
552	    summary keys survive. ``None`` sample passes through unchanged.
553	    """
554	    if not sample:
555	        return None
556	    safe = _safe_sample_columns(tested_column, policy)
557	    show_tested = tested_column is not None and tested_column in safe
558	    out: dict[str, Any] = {}
559	    for key, value in sample.items():
560	        if _is_safe_summary(key, value):
561	            out[key] = value

564	        elif key == "unexpected_index_list" and isinstance(value, list):
565	            out[key] = [_redact_row(row, safe) for row in value]
566	        else:
567	            out[key] = _redact_sample_value(value)
568	    return out

1	"""Shared Great Expectations machinery for the datasource `CheckRunner`s.
2	
3	The GX-version-specific translation — snake_case `expectation_type` → GX class,
4	and GX `ExpectationSuiteValidationResult` → our GX-agnostic `SuiteOutcome` DTOs —
5	is identical across datasources. It lives here so every runner (Snowflake table,
6	flat-file DataFrame, Unity Catalog later) reuses one implementation and the GX v1
7	API is pinned in a single place (CLAUDE.md §5 — GX has drifted across releases).
8	
9	Each runner only differs in how it builds the GX *batch* (a Snowflake table
10	asset vs an in-memory pandas asset); once it has a `batch_definition` it calls
11	`run_expectations`, which registers the suite + validation definition and maps
12	the result. Tests exercise these pure parts with constructed GX results and a
13	canned DataFrame — no live datasource required.
14	"""
15	
16	from __future__ import annotations
17	
18	from typing import Any
19	
20	import great_expectations as gx
21	import great_expectations.expectations as gxe
22	
23	from backend.app.datasources.base import CheckOutcome, CheckSpec, SuiteOutcome
24	
25	# GX result keys that describe failing rows — copied into CheckOutcome.sample_failures.
26	# These may contain real data, so they only ever reach logs via the redactor.
27	_SAMPLE_KEYS = ("partial_unexpected_list", "unexpected_count", "unexpected_percent")
28	
29	# GX injects internal bookkeeping keys into expectation_config.kwargs at run time
30	# (e.g. batch_id); strip them so expected_value persists only the check's own
31	# parameters.
32	_GX_INTERNAL_KWARGS = frozenset({"batch_id"})
33	
34	
35	class UnknownExpectationError(ValueError):
36	    """Raised when a check's expectation_type has no matching GX expectation."""
37	
38	
39	def _expectation_class_name(expectation_type: str) -> str:
40	    """snake_case GX type → PascalCase class name.
41	
42	    ``expect_column_values_to_not_be_null`` → ``ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull``.
43	    """
44	    return "".join(part.title() for part in expectation_type.split("_"))
45	
46	
47	def _to_gx_expectation(spec: CheckSpec) -> Any:
48	    class_name = _expectation_class_name(spec.expectation_type)
49	    expectation_cls = getattr(gxe, class_name, None)
50	    if expectation_cls is None:
51	        raise UnknownExpectationError(
52	            f"Unknown expectation_type {spec.expectation_type!r} (no gx class {class_name!r})"
53	        )
54	    return expectation_cls(**spec.kwargs)
55	
56	
57	def _extract_sample_failures(result: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
58	    sample = {key: result[key] for key in _SAMPLE_KEYS if key in result}
59	    return sample or None
60	
61	
62	def _check_errored(exception_info: Any) -> tuple[bool, str | None]:
63	    """Did this expectation raise while being evaluated? (GX `exception_info`).
64	
65	    GX (1.17) reports `exception_info` in two shapes per `ExpectationValidationResult`:
66	
67	    * a **flat** dict ``{'raised_exception': bool, 'exception_message': str|None,
68	      ...}`` for a cleanly-evaluated expectation, and
69	    * a dict **keyed by `MetricConfigurationID`** when a metric computation raised,
70	      each value being a flat dict with its own ``raised_exception``.
71	
72	    Treat the check as errored if the flat form raised, or any keyed entry did;
73	    return the first exception message for debuggability. An errored check is an
74	    ``error`` result (#122), not a data ``fail``.
75	    """
76	    if not isinstance(exception_info, dict) or not exception_info:
77	        return False, None
78	    if "raised_exception" in exception_info:  # flat shape
79	        return bool(exception_info.get("raised_exception")), exception_info.get("exception_message")
80	    # keyed-by-metric shape: errored if any metric computation raised
81	    for entry in exception_info.values():
82	        if isinstance(entry, dict) and entry.get("raised_exception"):
83	            return True, entry.get("exception_message")
84	    return False, None
85	
86	
87	def _expected_value(kwargs: Any) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
88	    cleaned = {key: value for key, value in dict(kwargs).items() if key not in _GX_INTERNAL_KWARGS}
89	    return cleaned or None
90	
91	
92	def to_suite_outcome(gx_result: Any) -> SuiteOutcome:
93	    """Map a GX ExpectationSuiteValidationResult onto our GX-agnostic DTO.
94	
95	    Kept GX-translation-only (no datasource specifics) so it is unit-testable
96	    with a constructed GX result, no live datasource required.
97	    """
98	    outcomes: list[CheckOutcome] = []
99	    for check_result in gx_result.results:
100	        config = check_result.expectation_config
101	        detail: dict[str, Any] = check_result.result or {}
102	        observed = (
103	            {"observed_value": detail["observed_value"]} if "observed_value" in detail else None
104	        )
105	        errored, error_message = _check_errored(getattr(check_result, "exception_info", None))
106	        outcomes.append(
107	            CheckOutcome(
108	                expectation_type=config.type,
109	                success=bool(check_result.success),
110	                observed_value=observed,
111	                expected_value=_expected_value(config.kwargs) if config.kwargs else None,
112	                sample_failures=_extract_sample_failures(detail),
113	                errored=errored,
114	                error_message=error_message,
115	            )
116	        )
117	    return SuiteOutcome(success=bool(gx_result.success), checks=outcomes)
118	
119	
120	def run_expectations(
121	    context: Any,
122	    *,
123	    batch_definition: Any,
124	    checks: list[CheckSpec],
125	    name: str,
126	    batch_parameters: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
127	) -> SuiteOutcome:
128	    """Register the suite + validation definition for `batch_definition` and run.
129	
130	    The shared tail of every runner: GX 1.x requires the suite and validation
131	    definition to be registered on the (ephemeral, per-run) context before
132	    ``run()``. `batch_parameters` carries the in-memory DataFrame for a pandas
133	    asset; it stays `None` for an asset that resolves its own batch (a SQL table),
134	    matching a bare ``run()``.
135	    """
136	    suite = context.suites.add(
137	        gx.ExpectationSuite(
138	            name=name,
139	            expectations=[_to_gx_expectation(check) for check in checks],
140	        )
141	    )
142	    validation_definition = context.validation_definitions.add(
143	        gx.ValidationDefinition(name=f"vd-{name}", data=batch_definition, suite=suite)
144	    )
145	    result = validation_definition.run(batch_parameters=batch_parameters, result_format="COMPLETE")
146	    return to_suite_outcome(result)
147

92	def _run_outcomes(
93	    runner: CheckRunner, *, table: str, schema: str | None, checks: list[Check]
94	) -> list[CheckOutcome]:
95	    """Run a suite's checks, dispatching by `check.kind` (ADR 0012), and return one
96	    outcome per check in the **same order** (so they zip 1:1 onto result rows).
97	
98	    * ``expectation`` kind → the GX `CheckRunner.run_checks`.
99	    * ``freshness``/``volume`` (monitor kinds) → the `MonitorRunner.run_monitors`
100	      SQL path — only when the runner is a SQL datasource (Snowflake/UC). A monitor
101	      check on a flat-file runner raises (gated here, not silently mis-run).
102	    * any other reserved kind (`schema_drift`/`anomaly`/`comparison`) has no runner
103	      yet → `NotImplementedError`.
104	
105	    This composes with the connection-type runner selection (ADR 0011): `kind`
106	    chooses the *monitor*, `connection.type` chose the *adapter* (the runner)."""
107	    expectation_idx = [i for i, c in enumerate(checks) if c.kind == _EXPECTATION_KIND]
108	    monitor_idx = [i for i, c in enumerate(checks) if c.kind in MONITOR_KINDS]
109	    unsupported = sorted(
110	        {c.kind for c in checks if c.kind != _EXPECTATION_KIND and c.kind not in MONITOR_KINDS}
111	    )
112	    if unsupported:
113	        raise NotImplementedError(f"no run path for check kind(s) {', '.join(unsupported)}")
114	
115	    outcomes: list[CheckOutcome | None] = [None] * len(checks)
116	    if expectation_idx:
117	        specs = [
118	            CheckSpec(expectation_type=checks[i].expectation_type, kwargs=dict(checks[i].config))
119	            for i in expectation_idx
120	        ]
121	        suite_outcome = runner.run_checks(table=table, schema=schema, checks=specs)
122	        for i, oc in zip(expectation_idx, suite_outcome.checks, strict=True):
123	            outcomes[i] = oc
124	    if monitor_idx:
125	        if not isinstance(runner, MonitorRunner):
126	            raise NotImplementedError(
127	                f"{type(runner).__name__} does not support monitor checks — "
128	                "freshness/volume need a SQL datasource (Snowflake / Unity Catalog)"
129	            )
130	        monitors = [
131	            MonitorSpec(kind=checks[i].kind, config=dict(checks[i].config)) for i in monitor_idx
132	        ]
133	        monitor_outcomes = runner.run_monitors(table=table, schema=schema, monitors=monitors)
134	        for i, oc in zip(monitor_idx, monitor_outcomes, strict=True):
135	            outcomes[i] = oc
136	
137	    # Every index is filled: expectation_idx + monitor_idx together cover all checks
138	    # once the unsupported-kind guard above has run.
139	    return [cast(CheckOutcome, oc) for oc in outcomes]

155	def execute_run(
156	    session: Session,
157	    *,
158	    run: Run,
159	    checks: list[Check],
160	    runner: CheckRunner,
161	    table: str,
162	    schema: str | None = None,
163	) -> Run:
164	    """Run ``checks`` against ``table`` via ``runner`` and persist the outcome.
165	
166	    ``run`` must already be persisted (it carries the id the results link to).
167	    Returns the same `Run`, updated to ``succeeded`` or ``failed``.
168	    """
169	    run.status = "running"
170	    run.started_at = _now()
171	    session.commit()
172	    log.info(
173	        "run_started",
174	        run_id=str(run.id),
175	        suite_id=str(run.suite_id),
176	        n_checks=len(checks),
177	        table=table,
178	    )
179	
180	    # Everything from here — dispatching by kind, running the adapter, building
181	    # rows, and persisting them — is guarded so any failure drives the run to a
182	    # terminal 'failed' state. Without this, a DB error during add_all/commit (or
183	    # an unrunnable check kind) would leave the run stuck in 'running' forever.
184	    # rollback() discards any partial result inserts before we record the failure.
185	    try:
186	        outcomes = _run_outcomes(runner, table=table, schema=schema, checks=checks)
187	        rows = [
188	            _build_result(run.id, check, check_outcome)
189	            for check, check_outcome in zip(checks, outcomes, strict=True)
190	        ]
191	        session.add_all(rows)
192	        # Cooperative cancellation: if a cancel committed (from the API session)
193	        # while GX ran, don't overwrite it with a terminal success — drop the now-
194	        # moot (still-pending, unflushed) results and leave the run 'cancelled'.
195	        if _cancelled_mid_run(session, run):
196	            session.rollback()
197	            log.info("run_cancelled_during_execution", run_id=str(run.id))
198	            return run
199	        run.status = "succeeded"
200	        run.finished_at = _now()
201	        session.commit()
202	    except Exception:
203	        session.rollback()
204	        # Same cooperative check on the failure path: a run the user cancelled
205	        # mid-flight that *also* errored stays 'cancelled', not masked as 'failed'.
206	        if _cancelled_mid_run(session, run):
207	            log.info("run_cancelled_during_execution", run_id=str(run.id))
208	            return run
209	        run.status = "failed"
210	        run.finished_at = _now()
211	        session.commit()
212	        log.exception("run_failed", run_id=str(run.id), table=table)
213	        return run
214	
215	    log.info(
216	        "run_completed",
217	        run_id=str(run.id),
218	        suite_success=all(o.success for o in outcomes),
219	        n_results=len(rows),
220	    )
221	    return run

> AGENT

Key finding: a **missing index column doesn't raise at `run()`** — it marks every expectation `errored` (the index-metric fails for each). So a bad/drifted identifier would flip the whole suite to errored. I'll add an **all-errored fallback** (re-run without the index) as a safety net, plus validate the identifier in the setter (increment 4). Let me confirm the read path already passes `tested_column`+`policy` (from #417) so the captured identifier actually surfaces.

  "old_string": "def run_expectations(\n    context: Any,\n    *,\n    batch_definition: Any,\n    checks: list[CheckSpec],\n    name: str,\n    batch_parameters: dict[str, Any] | None = None,\n) -> SuiteOutcome:\n    \"\"\"Register the suite + validation definition for `batch_definition` and run.\n\n    The shared tail of every runner: GX 1.x requires the suite and validation\n    definition to be registered on the (ephemeral, per-run) context before\n    ``run()``. `batch_parameters` carries the in-memory DataFrame for a pandas\n    asset; it stays `None` for an asset that resolves its own batch (a SQL table),\n    matching a bare ``run()``.\n    \"\"\"\n    suite = context.suites.add(\n        gx.ExpectationSuite(\n            name=name,\n            expectations=[_to_gx_expectation(check) for check in checks],\n        )\n    )\n    validation_definition = context.validation_definitions.add(\n        gx.ValidationDefinition(name=f\"vd-{name}\", data=batch_definition, suite=suite)\n    )\n    result = validation_definition.run(batch_parameters=batch_parameters, result_format=\"COMPLETE\")\n    return to_suite_outcome(result)",
  "new_string": "def _execute(\n    context: Any,\n    *,\n    batch_definition: Any,\n    checks: list[CheckSpec],\n    name: str,\n    batch_parameters: dict[str, Any] | None,\n    result_format: Any,\n) -> SuiteOutcome:\n    \"\"\"Register the suite + validation definition (GX 1.x requires both on the\n    ephemeral per-run context before ``run()``) and map the result.\"\"\"\n    suite = context.suites.add(\n        gx.ExpectationSuite(\n            name=name,\n            expectations=[_to_gx_expectation(check) for check in checks],\n        )\n    )\n    validation_definition = context.validation_definitions.add(\n        gx.ValidationDefinition(name=f\"vd-{name}\", data=batch_definition, suite=suite)\n    )\n    result = validation_definition.run(batch_parameters=batch_parameters, result_format=result_format)\n    return to_suite_outcome(result)\n\n\ndef run_expectations(\n    context: Any,\n    *,\n    batch_definition: Any,\n    checks: list[CheckSpec],\n    name: str,\n    batch_parameters: dict[str, Any] | None = None,\n    index_columns: list[str] | None = None,\n) -> SuiteOutcome:\n    \"\"\"Register the suite + validation definition for `batch_definition` and run.\n\n    The shared tail of every runner. `batch_parameters` carries the in-memory\n    DataFrame for a pandas asset; it stays `None` for an asset that resolves its own\n    batch (a SQL table), matching a bare ``run()``.\n\n    ``index_columns`` (#415) requests GX's ``unexpected_index_column_names`` so each\n    failing row is returned as a dict carrying those identifier column(s) + the failing\n    value — the locator the redactor can surface. GX evaluates the index metric per\n    expectation, so a **bad/absent** identifier column errors *every* check; we detect\n    that (all checks errored, only when an index was requested) and fall back to a plain\n    run, so the checks still evaluate — just without the row identifier.\n    \"\"\"\n    if not index_columns:\n        return _execute(\n            context,\n            batch_definition=batch_definition,\n            checks=checks,\n            name=name,\n            batch_parameters=batch_parameters,\n            result_format=\"COMPLETE\",\n        )\n    outcome = _execute(\n        context,\n        batch_definition=batch_definition,\n        checks=checks,\n        name=name,\n        batch_parameters=batch_parameters,\n        result_format={\"result_format\": \"COMPLETE\", \"unexpected_index_column_names\": index_columns},\n    )\n    if outcome.checks and all(check.errored for check in outcome.checks):\n        return _execute(\n            context,\n            batch_definition=batch_definition,\n            checks=checks,\n            name=f\"{name}-noidx\",\n            batch_parameters=batch_parameters,\n            result_format=\"COMPLETE\",\n        )\n    return outcome"

    def run_checks(
        self,
        *,
        table: str,
        schema: str | None,
        checks: list[CheckSpec],
    ) -> SuiteOutcome:
        context = gx.get_context(mode="ephemeral")
        add_kwargs: dict[str, Any] = {}
        if self._connect_args:
            # GX 1.17 deprecates passing private_key via kwargs['connect_args'] in
            # favour of a direct private_key= arg; this works today but should
            # migrate during the live-Snowflake smoke (#195). The adapter test +
            # profiler paths use create_engine directly, so they're unaffected.
            add_kwargs["kwargs"] = {"connect_args": self._connect_args}
        datasource = context.data_sources.add_snowflake(
            name=f"sf-{table}",
            connection_string=self._connection_string,
            **add_kwargs,
        )
        asset = datasource.add_table_asset(
            name=table,
            table_name=table,
            schema_name=schema or self._config.schema_,
        )
        # The table asset resolves its own batch, so no batch_parameters; the
        # ephemeral context makes the fixed suite/vd names safe across runs.
        batch_definition = asset.add_batch_definition_whole_table(name="whole_table")
        return run_expectations(
            context, batch_definition=batch_definition, checks=checks, name=f"suite-{table}"
        )

    def run_monitors(
        self, *, table: str, schema: str | None, monitors: list[MonitorSpec]
    ) -> list[CheckOutcome]:
=== flatfile run_checks ===
    def run_checks(
        self, *, table: str, schema: str | None, checks: list[CheckSpec]
    ) -> SuiteOutcome:

        )
        context = gx.get_context(mode="ephemeral")
        asset = context.data_sources.add_pandas(name="flatfile").add_dataframe_asset(name="file")
        # The pandas asset takes its batch at run time via batch_parameters; the

        batch_definition = asset.add_batch_definition_whole_dataframe(name="whole_dataframe")

            batch_definition=batch_definition,
            checks=checks,
            name="suite-flatfile",
            batch_parameters={"dataframe": df},
        )

```
1	"""Column profiler — per-column statistics for the check editor.
2	
3	Given a target (a SQL table or a flat file) and a set of columns on a suite's
4	connection, compute the stats an author needs before writing expectations: row
5	count, null count / fraction, distinct count, min / max, and the most frequent
6	values. Persists nothing — a read-only authoring aid (the check-editor "profile
7	on table/file select" panel).
8	
9	`profile_connection` dispatches on the connection type:
10	
11	* **SQL datasources** (Snowflake + Unity Catalog) — aggregate the stats
12	  in-warehouse with one round-trip + a top-values query per column, via the
13	  datasource's SQLAlchemy dialect. Unity Catalog adds a `catalog` so the table is
14	  qualified `catalog.schema.table` (3-level namespace); Snowflake is `schema.table`.
15	* **Flat-file datasources** (ADLS Gen2, S3) — download a *sample* of the file
16	  (`_SAMPLE_ROWS` rows) into Pandas and compute the same stats locally. CSV and
17	  Parquet are supported; stats are therefore over the sample, not the whole file.
18	
19	**SQL-injection safety.** For SQL datasources, table / schema / column names are
20	caller-supplied and become SQL *identifiers* (they can't be bound parameters).
21	Queries are built with the SQLAlchemy Core expression language (`select` /
22	`table` / `column`) — never string formatting — so the dialect does the quoting
23	and there is no raw-SQL sink. As defence-in-depth (and a clean early 422) each
24	identifier is also validated against a strict allowlist. Flat-file columns are
25	checked for existence against the loaded frame instead (a missing column is a
26	clean 422, and Pandas indexing never builds SQL).
27	
28	Like the GX adapter, the pure pieces (identifier validation, query building,
29	dataframe profiling, result assembly) are unit-testable without a live
30	datasource; the I/O seams (`_open_connection`, `_read_dataframe`) are
31	monkeypatched in tests, and a live smoke is deferred.
32	"""
33

62	# Formats the profiler can actually parse. NOT redundant with
63	# flatfile.format_from_path (which only recognises path extensions): this also
64	# validates the caller's `explicit` file_format override (an arbitrary string),
65	# and is deliberately a *subset* of recognised formats — a format can be
66	# recognised by path yet unsupported here, which should still 422 (#147).
67	_SUPPORTED_FORMATS = {"csv", "parquet"}
68	# Flat-file profiling reads at most this many rows — stats are over the sample.
69	_SAMPLE_ROWS = 100_000
70	
71	# A plain SQL identifier: letter/underscore start, then letters/digits/_/$ (the
72	# Snowflake unquoted-identifier set). Anything else (spaces, quotes, dots, etc.)
73	# is refused — it can't be made injection-safe by quoting alone here.
74	_IDENTIFIER = re.compile(r"^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_$]*$")
75	
76	# Connector timeouts (seconds): fail fast rather than hang the request thread.
77	_LOGIN_TIMEOUT = 10
78	_NETWORK_TIMEOUT = 30
79

82	    status_code = 422
83	    code = "profile_unsupported"

86	class ProfileTargetInvalidError(DataQError):
87	    status_code = 422
88	    code = "profile_target_invalid"
89

92	    status_code = 422
93	    code = "profile_identifier_invalid"
94	
95	
96	class ProfileColumnNotFoundError(DataQError):
97	    status_code = 422
98	    code = "profile_column_not_found"
99	
100	
101	class ProfileFailedError(DataQError):
102	    status_code = 502
103	    code = "profile_failed"

106	@dataclass(frozen=True)
107	class ColumnProfile:
108	    column: str
109	    null_count: int
110	    null_fraction: float
111	    distinct_count: int | None  # None when the column's values aren't hashable
112	    min_value: Any
113	    max_value: Any
114	    top_values: list[dict[str, Any]]  # [{"value": ..., "count": int}]
115	
116	
117	@dataclass(frozen=True)
118	class ProfileResult:
119	    """A profiled target. Identity fields are type-specific: SQL datasources set
120	    `table` / `schema`, flat-file datasources set `path` / `file_format`."""
121	
122	    row_count: int
123	    columns: list[ColumnProfile]
124	    table: str | None = None
125	    schema: str | None = None
126	    catalog: str | None = None
127	    path: str | None = None
128	    file_format: str | None = None
129	
130	
131	# ───────────────────────── shared stat contract ────────────────────
132	
133	
134	def null_fraction(null_count: int, row_count: int) -> float:
135	    """Fraction of rows that are null, guarding the empty-target divide-by-zero.
136	
137	    The one stat definition the SQL profiler (`assemble_profile`) and the pandas
138	    profiler (`profile_dataframe`) can actually share — both must agree that a
139	    0-row target reports `0.0`, not `1.0` or a `ZeroDivisionError` (#147). The
140	    other contract points (distinct excludes nulls; top values are non-null,
141	    highest-count-first) are structurally SQL-vs-pandas and can't share code, so
142	    they're pinned by the parallel-path tests instead.
143	    """
144	    return (null_count / row_count) if row_count else 0.0
145	
146	
147	# ───────────────────────── pure query builders ─────────────────────
148	
149	
150	def validate_identifier(name: str | None) -> str:
151	    """Validate `name` against the plain-identifier allowlist and return it.
152	
153	    Raises `ProfileIdentifierInvalidError` (422) for anything that isn't a plain
154	    identifier. The SQLAlchemy Core builders quote safely on their own; this is
155	    defence-in-depth and turns an odd name into a clean 422 instead of a quoted
156	    column that simply doesn't exist.
157	    """
158	    if not name or not _IDENTIFIER.match(name):
159	        raise ProfileIdentifierInvalidError(
160	            "not a valid table/schema/column identifier", detail={"identifier": name}
161	        )
162	    return name
163	
164	
165	def _table(schema: str, table_name: str, catalog: str | None = None) -> Any:
166	    """A Core table clause, optionally with a 3-level namespace (Unity Catalog).
167	
168	    With a `catalog`, the namespace is `catalog.schema` passed as an unquoted
169	    `quoted_name` so the dialect emits three dotted parts (`catalog.schema.table`)
170	    rather than quoting the dotted string as one identifier. Safe because every
171	    part is allowlist-validated.
172	    """
173	    validate_identifier(schema)
174	    if catalog is not None:
175	        validate_identifier(catalog)
176	        namespace: Any = quoted_name(f"{catalog}.{schema}", quote=False)
177	    else:
178	        namespace = schema
179	    return table(validate_identifier(table_name), schema=namespace)
180	
181	
182	def build_aggregate_query(
183	    schema: str, table_name: str, columns: list[str], catalog: str | None = None
184	) -> Select[Any]:
185	    """One round-trip: row count + null/distinct/min/max per column.
186	
187	    Built with the Core expression language (no string SQL); identifiers are
188	    validated then handed to `column()`/`table()`, which the dialect quotes.
189	    """
190	    projection: list[Any] = [func.count().label("row_count")]
191	    for i, col in enumerate(columns):
192	        c: Any = column(validate_identifier(col))
193	        projection.append((func.count() - func.count(c)).label(f"nulls_{i}"))
194	        projection.append(func.count(distinct(c)).label(f"distinct_{i}"))
195	        projection.append(func.min(c).label(f"min_{i}"))
196	        projection.append(func.max(c).label(f"max_{i}"))
197	    return select(*projection).select_from(_table(schema, table_name, catalog))
198	
199	
200	def build_top_values_query(
201	    schema: str, table_name: str, col: str, top_n: int, catalog: str | None = None
202	) -> Select[Any]:
203	    """Most frequent non-null values for one column (highest count first)."""
204	    c: Any = column(validate_identifier(col))
205	    freq = func.count().label("freq")
206	    return (
207	        select(c.label("value"), freq)
208	        .select_from(_table(schema, table_name, catalog))
209	        .where(c.is_not(None))
210	        .group_by(c)
211	        .order_by(func.count().desc(), c)
212	        .limit(int(top_n))
213	    )
214	
215	
216	def build_columns_query(schema: str, table_name: str, catalog: str | None = None) -> Select[Any]:
217	    """List a target's column names: `SELECT * FROM <target> LIMIT 0`.
218	
219	    Returns no rows, but the cursor still exposes the column names via
220	    `result.keys()` — so it's a cheap, dialect-agnostic way to introspect columns
221	    that reuses the same catalog-aware, allowlist-validated `_table` namespace as
222	    the profiler (rather than the SQLAlchemy inspector, which is fiddly for Unity
223	    Catalog's 3-level `catalog.schema.table`). `literal_column("*")` is a SQL
224	    constant, not caller input — the only caller-supplied parts go through
225	    `_table`'s identifier validation.
226	    """
227	    return select(literal_column("*")).select_from(_table(schema, table_name, catalog)).limit(0)
228	
229	
230	def assemble_profile(
231	    *,
232	    table: str,
233	    schema: str,
234	    columns: list[str],
235	    aggregate: Mapping[str, Any],
236	    top_values: dict[str, list[Mapping[str, Any]]],
237	    catalog: str | None = None,
238	) -> ProfileResult:
239	    """Build the `ProfileResult` from raw query rows (pure, warehouse-free)."""
240	    row_count = int(aggregate["row_count"])
241	    profiles: list[ColumnProfile] = []
242	    for i, col in enumerate(columns):
243	        nulls = int(aggregate[f"nulls_{i}"])
244	        profiles.append(
245	            ColumnProfile(
246	                column=col,
247	                null_count=nulls,
248	                null_fraction=null_fraction(nulls, row_count),
249	                distinct_count=int(aggregate[f"distinct_{i}"]),
250	                min_value=sanitize_json(aggregate[f"min_{i}"]),
251	                max_value=sanitize_json(aggregate[f"max_{i}"]),
252	                top_values=[
253	                    {"value": sanitize_json(r["value"]), "count": int(r["freq"])}
254	                    for r in top_values.get(col, [])
255	                ],
256	            )
257	        )
258	    return ProfileResult(
259	        table=table, schema=schema, catalog=catalog, row_count=row_count, columns=profiles
260	    )
261

263	# ───────────────────────── profiler registry ───────────────────────
264	#
265	# One table maps connection.type to its profiling strategy, so adding a
266	# datasource is a single entry here — not edits scattered across the type sets,
267	# `_engine_args`, and `profile_connection` (#146). SQL types carry their engine
268	# builder + whether they need a `catalog`; flat-file types are uniform (the
269	# object-store backend, S3 vs ADLS, is dispatched inside `flatfile`).
270	
271	
272	def _snowflake_engine_args(connection: Connection, secret: str) -> tuple[str, dict[str, Any]]:
273	    sf = SnowflakeConfig.model_validate(connection.config)
274	    return build_connection_string(sf, secret), {
275	        "login_timeout": _LOGIN_TIMEOUT,
276	        "network_timeout": _NETWORK_TIMEOUT,
277	        # Key-pair auth threads the private key in as a connect-arg (empty for password).
278	        **build_connect_args(sf, secret),
279	    }
280	
281	
282	def _unity_catalog_engine_args(connection: Connection, secret: str) -> tuple[str, dict[str, Any]]:
283	    cfg = UnityCatalogConfig.model_validate(connection.config)
284	    # Catalog is not pinned on the URL — the profiler query qualifies the full
285	    # catalog.schema.table namespace itself (see `_table`).
286	    return build_databricks_url(cfg, secret), {}
